chunks: Adding motor braking to a drive. The question: What if you need motor braking?
A single switch can only let a motor coast, so it slows down on friction, which can take seconds.
To brake, you give the motor's own generated voltage a path to push current through.
The simplest way is to connect the motor's two terminals together by turning on the drive's bottom (low-side) switches.
The motor then works as a generator into its own winding and slows itself down. This braking is strong at high speed and fades to nothing at standstill.
Picture a spinning merry-go-round with a paddle dipped in thick syrup. The faster it spins, the harder the syrup pushes back, and as it slows, the drag fades.
It slows quickly at first and then creeps to a stop. A shorted motor is that paddle, and the drag grows in proportion to speed.
Coasting barely slows in 0. 4 seconds. Dynamic braking falls exponentially (95% of the speed gone in about 0.
14 seconds) but the last bit is slow because torque vanishes with speed.
A current-limited plugging stop has constant deceleration and reaches zero in about 52 milliseconds, but only if the drive switches off exactly then.
Model: J equals 2 times 10 to the -5 kg·m², K equals 0. 02 , R equals 1 ohms , b equals 2 times 10 to the -5 N·m·s/rad.
Coast: both terminals open. Only friction slows the motor. Dynamic braking: shorting the terminals, so the motor's back-EMF drives a current that opposes the rotation.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, E equals K e omega . Plugging: applying reverse drive voltage while spinning forward. It brakes harder but is riskier.
A motor has K e equals 0. 02 volts per rad/s and a 1 ohms winding, and spins at 3000 rpm, or 314 rad/s. Its back-EMF is 0. 02 times 314 equals 6. 28 volts.
Short the terminals and the brake current starts at 6. 28 over 1 equals 6. 28 amps.
For a small rotor, the speed then falls to about 37% every 48 milliseconds (the time constant), against about 1 seconds when coasting.
Plugging with 12 volts reversed would start at (12 plus 6. 28) over 1 equals 18. 3 amps and must be cut at zero speed, or the motor spins backward. That is the whole idea.
"A single low-side switch can only coast.
To brake I give the motor's back-EMF a short-circuit path: in a half-bridge, turn on the low-side FET; in an H-bridge, turn on both low sides.
The motor then acts as a generator into its own resistance and stops in a time constant of tens of milliseconds instead of seconds.
I'd check the brake current, E over R, against FET and winding ratings, limit it with PWM if needed, and remember braking has no holding torque at standstill."
